docs.title: What Is Web3? Understanding the Next Generation of the Internet
docs.text: Since you've picked this article, I'm sure you've heard about Web3 several times. You've probably seen stuff about it on Twitter or the news, or you might have even heard about it from that airdrop-obsessed friend who keeps sending you links. Even with all this information about it, you're probably still confused. We all are at first. Worry no more cause you're reading the right article. This article covers what you need to know about Web3 as a beginner or a curious mind. However, you wouldn't be a crypto guru after reading this article. You'll be more enlightened and educated on Web3 when you've finished. Let's dive in.

docs.title: The Internet in phases
docs.text:
To truly understand Web3 and why it matters, it helps to look at how the Web has evolved. The Web didn't always contain social media, apps, and content creators making a living online. The internet has gone through several key phases, each marking a shift in how we interact with information and each other. These phases are known as Web1, Web2, and now, Web3.

Web1 was the first generation of the web. As nice as it seemed in the early 1990s when it was adopted, Web1 was associated with many restrictions. It consisted of static web pages and was named the "Static web" or the "Read-only web".Web1 didn't contain user-generated content, and there was little to no interactivity. Information only flowed one way, from the publisher to the user.

Web2 is the second generation of the Web became widely adopted around 2004. This era brought about the launching and rise of social media platforms like Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter. In the late 2000s, it brought the rapid rise of smartphones, apps, user-generated content, and cloud services. Web2 also saw the creation of interactive websites, ad-driven business models, and real-time communication(e.g.comments, likes, video calls, live streams, etc.). Even though it has been around for decades, Web2 is still the dominant model today.

Web3 is the third generation of the web. Its development began around 2014. It differs from the previous generations of the web because it allows users to own their data and digital assets. So, not only do you get to generate content, you also get to own it. It focuses on privacy and transparency.

Now that we’ve seen where Web3 fits in the evolution of the internet, let’s take a closer look at what makes it so different and why it's gathering so much attention.

docs.title: What is Web3
docs.text: Web3 is the next generation of the internet, built on blockchain technology, the same tech that powers cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum. At its core, Blockchain is a special kind of database, a digital ledger that records information in a way that’s secure, transparent, and can’t be changed. What makes Web3 different is that it allows users to own their data, control their digital identity, and even hold a stake in the platforms they use without relying on centralized companies. So, what exactly makes Web3 different from the internet you’re used to? Let’s break down its key traits.

docs.title: Key characteristics
docs.text:
Web3 isn’t just a new version of the internet, it’s a fundamental shift in how digital systems are built and who controls them. Let’s explore the defining traits that make Web3 so different from what came before.

  • Decentralization In Web3, no single company controls the entire platform. Instead, it runs on blockchain network systems spread across many computers. This means no one person or company has total control.

  • User ownership With Web3, you truly own your data and digital assets. Instead of companies storing and controlling your information, it stays with you, often in a digital wallet only you can access.

  • Cryptocurrency Web3 uses digital money called cryptocurrencies (like Bitcoin or Ethereum) for transactions. These let you send or receive money directly, without needing a bank or payment service.

  • Transparency Everything that happens on a blockchain is open and visible. You can see where money goes, how apps work, and what rules they follow building more trust in the system.

  • No Middlemen Web3 apps use smart contracts, pieces of code that automatically do what they’re told. This removes the need for third parties like banks, lawyers, or companies to approve actions.

  • Open access Anyone with an internet connection and a digital wallet can join the Web3 world. You don’t need permission to use apps, trade assets, or be part of a community.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Web3 matters because it shifts the control of the internet from big companies to individual users. Web3 gives people ownership of their data, assets, and digital identity. It opens up financial access globally, builds trust through transparency, and enables new ways to work and create online without needing permission from Middlemen. Ultimately, Web3 offers a more open, fair, and user-powered internet.

docs.title: What’s next
docs.text: Web3 might sound like a big buzzword, but at its heart, it’s about making the internet better for everyone. It gives you more control over your data, digital stuff, and how you interact online, all powered by blockchain and tools like cryptocurrencies. We’re still in the early days, but Web3 is opening doors to a more open, fair, and creative internet, where you’re not just a user but a participant. Whether you’re here to learn, explore, or maybe even build, Web3 is a space that welcomes beginners and big ideas alike.

docs.title: What is Aptos? A Beginner-Friendly Introduction
docs.text:
In the Web2 version of the internet, which is probably the version you’re familiar with, services such as messaging, finance, shopping or even gaming are provided by a centralized entity which owns and controls direct access to user data.

This is why the Web3 version of the internet emerged with blockchains, which provide unchangeable and shared digital records, giving users direct control and access over their own data.

The Aptos blockchain is a secure and superfast modern blockchain created by former Facebook engineers (now Meta). The Aptos vision is to deliver a blockchain that can bring mainstream adoption to Web3 and empower an ecosystem of decentralized applications to solve real-world user problems.

docs.title: Why is Aptos Different?
docs.text:
Despite the existence of many blockchains today, Web3 has still not been adopted widely. This is the gap Aptos is trying to bridge.

Many existing blockchains are expensive, slow, or not secure enough for mainstream use The Aptos mission is to advance blockchain reliability, safety, and performance. Aptos aims to support: frequent upgrades, fast adoption of new technology,and support for emerging use cases.

Aptos focuses on security, speed, and affordability.

docs.title: What Makes Aptos Special?
docs.text:
Aptos is built from scratch to satisfy specific blockchain needs. It has its own:

  • Programming language (Move)
  • Unique design
  • Novel method for confirming transactions

Aptos uses the Move language, a new smart contract programming language focused on safety and flexibility. Move is inspired by the Rust programming language (used by Solana) and emphasizes: resource scarcity, preservation and access control. It also uses a fast and secure consensus mechanism called AptosBFT, which helps all computers agree even if a few go offline

Aptos is designed to be faster, safer, and smarter compared to other blockchains.

docs.title: What Can You Do With It?
docs.text:
No matter who you are or what you do, Aptos opens up a lot of possibilities. Whether you're a user, builder, or just curious, there’s always something to do on Aptos:

  • Use Aptos wallets to send/receive tokens, sign into Web3 platforms, or store NFTs
  • Explore decentralized apps on Aptos (e.g., gaming, social platforms, DeFi)
  • Learn the Move language as a developer or technical writer to build your own dApps
  • Stake tokens or help process transactions

docs.title: Why I’m Learning About Aptos
docs.text:
The future of the internet is Web3. I believe blockchain systems that grant you the freedom to build, improve, or just learn are the best way to integrate into Web3.

I aspire to be a Web3 technical writer, and I’m particularly drawn to Aptos because it offers exciting opportunities for growth, innovation, and meaningful contribution.

docs.title: First Steps into Web3 & Solidity
docs.text:
September 2, 2025

Today officially marks the start of my From Scratch journey into blockchain development. My goal is to learn daily, document everything I understand (and don’t understand), and keep track of my growth in both technical knowledge and personal reflections.

For Day 1, I decided to dive in with two popular beginner-friendly resources: - LearnWeb3: a structured curriculum that introduces blockchain and Web3 concepts step by step. - CryptoZombies: an interactive game-like tutorial that teaches Solidity through building a zombie-themed dApp.

I also set up a brand-new crypto wallet, experimented with faucets (more on that later), and even tried deploying my first smart contract.

docs.title: Starting Out with LearnWeb3
docs.text:
I kicked things off today with LearnWeb3, which is designed to guide beginners into blockchain development step by step. At first, it felt like a friendly introduction, covering the basics of programming, what a blockchain is, and what Web3 really means.

The pace was steady, but as I got deeper—especially when it came to Solidity and building my first dApp—things started to feel a little overwhelming. Still, I tried to take notes carefully, almost like I was building my own schoolbook on Web3.

docs.title: What is Programming?
docs.text: Programming is basically telling a computer what to do using a language it understands. Just like humans use English, Yoruba, or French to communicate, computers have their own “languages” like Python, JavaScript, or Solidity.

docs.title: What is a Blockchain?
docs.text:
A blockchain is a distributed and decentralized ledger that records transactions in a series of blocks linked together using cryptographic hashes.

In simpler terms, a blockchain is a digital ledger (like a notebook) that’s shared across many computers. Instead of one person keeping the records, everyone holds a copy, so it’s almost impossible to secretly alter it.

docs.title: What is Web3?
docs.text:
Web3 is the version of the internet where applications run on blockchains and are community-owned rather than controlled by a single centralized entity.

Put simply, it’s like moving from a classroom where one teacher controls the lesson (Web2) to a group project where everyone participates and has a say. This structure allows for shared ownership, transparency, and collaboration.

docs.title: What is Ethereum?
docs.text:
Ethereum is a decentralized, open-source blockchain platform that supports smart contracts and enables the creation of decentralized applications (dApps).

In simpler terms, Ethereum is like a global computer that anyone can use. Instead of relying on a single company’s servers, people all over the world contribute their computers to run programs and applications, making it more open, secure, and resistant to control by one authority.

docs.title: Setting Up a Crypto Wallet
docs.text:
To interact with Ethereum and Web3 applications, the first step was setting up a crypto wallet.

I used MetaMask, one of the most popular non-custodial wallets. MetaMask works as a browser extension and mobile app, allowing you to securely store your private keys and manage ETH and tokens. After setup, the wallet can connect directly to decentralized applications (dApps) with just a few clicks, making it a gateway to the Ethereum ecosystem.

👉 Official MetaMask setup guide

docs.title: Introduction to Solidity & My First dApp
docs.text:
Solidity is the programming language used to build smart contracts on Ethereum, the foundation of decentralized applications (dApps). Unlike traditional applications, dApps run on the blockchain, meaning once deployed, they are immutable. This makes testing and careful deployment especially important.

While building my first dApp, I experienced both excitement and challenges:

  • 🎉 My joy was unmatched when I finally discovered a faucet that allowed me to use a completely new wallet to receive testnet tokens (shoutout to Google Cloud Web3).
  • 😅 Deployment proved to be a headache, but it finally worked—it turned out to be a network issue.

For now, I’ve decided to pause my LearnWeb3 lessons until I gain a stronger grasp of Solidity itself. Taking things step by step feels like the right approach to build a solid foundation.

docs.title: CryptoZombies
docs.text:
After wrestling with LearnWeb3 and realizing I need a deeper grip on Solidity, I decided to switch things up and dive into CryptoZombies.

The introduction immediately felt different: less formal, more playful. Instead of throwing me into dense documentation, it frames Solidity through building a zombie game.

To make things more convenient and relatable, I adjusted the original CryptoZombies example. Instead of a Zombie Factory, I built a simple Pet Factory contract that creates pets with unique DNA. The structure and concepts are the same, but the new theme makes it easier to understand without the “zombie” flavor.

Now let’s break it down step by step…

docs.title: Version Declaration
docs.text:
pragma solidity >=0.5.0 <0.6.0;
  • This line tells the compiler which version of Solidity can compile this code.
  • It means: “This contract works with Solidity versions starting from 0.5.0 up to (but not including) 0.6.0.”

docs.title: Contract Definition
docs.text:
contract PetFactory {

}

  • A contract in Solidity is like a class in other languages.It contains state variables, functions, and events.

  • Here, we name the contract PetFactory.

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
event NewPet(uint petId, string name, uint dna);

  • Events are like logs that get recorded on the blockchain.They let external apps (like web apps) know when something happens.

  • We create a new pet, we fire an event with its ID, name, and DNA

docs.title: State Variables
docs.text:
uint dnaDigits = 16;
uint dnaModulus = 10 ** dnaDigits;

  • dnaDigits: We decide the length of the pet’s DNA → 16 digits.

  • dnaModulus: Makes sure our DNA doesn’t exceed 16 digits. (e.g., if a number is too big, % dnaModulus keeps it within range).

docs.title: Struct
docs.text:
uint dnaDigits = 16;
struct Pet {
    string name;
    uint dna;
}
  • Structs let us create custom data types.
  • Here a Pet has:
    • a name (string)
    • a dna (unique number that represents its traits).

docs.title: Array of Pets
docs.text:
Pet[] public pets;

  • This creates a dynamic array to store all pets

  • It’s marked public, so Solidity automatically gives us a getter function (i.e Anyone can check what pets exist.)

docs.title: Internal Create Function
docs.text:
function _createPet(string memory _name, uint _dna) private {
    uint id = pets.push(Pet(_name, _dna)) - 1;
    emit NewPet(id, _name, _dna);
}
  • _createPet: A private function (only usable inside the contract)
  • What it does:
    • Push a new Pet into the pets array
    • id = index of the new pet
    • Emit an event to let the outside world know the pet was created

docs.title: Random DNA Generator
docs.text:
function _generateRandomDna(string memory _str) private view returns (uint) {
    uint rand = uint(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_str)));
    return rand % dnaModulus;
}
  • _generateRandomDna: Generates a pseudo-random number from a string input.
  • Uses keccak256 (a hashing function in Ethereum).
  • dnaModulus ensures DNA is always 16 digits.
  • Marked view because it doesn’t change the blockchain, just reads from it.

docs.title: Public Function to Create Pets
docs.text:
function createRandomPet(string memory _name) public {
    uint randDna = _generateRandomDna(_name);
    _createPet(_name, randDna);
}
  • This is the main entry point for users
  • Anyone can call createRandomPet("Fluffy"), and it will:
    1. Generate a DNA from the name
    2. Create the new pet
    3. Save it to the blockchain and emit an event.

docs.title: Closing Thoughts on Day 1
docs.text:
Day 1 is done, and honestly, I feel proud. Solidity has always felt like a mountain, but breaking it down into pieces made it much less intimidating. It’s the first time I didn’t just copy-paste code but actually understood why it works.

For anyone who wants to take the same path, here are a few resources I found useful:

  • CryptoZombies – learn by building your own zombie game
  • Solidity Docs – best for clarifying syntax
  • FreeCodeCamp Solidity Tutorial – step-by-step video guide

docs.title: Taking a Step Back to Start Strong
docs.text:
September 3, 2025

This is day 2 of my From Scratch series, where I’ll be documenting my programming and blockchain development journey. My approach is actually quite simple: master the fundamentals before moving on.

Yesterday I jumped right into Solidity, but today I’ve decided not to skip anything. I’ll first complete a 3-week JavaScript course, then move on to a 7-week Ethereum bootcamp from Alchemy University, and finally revisit CryptoZombies. I hope this approach will help me achieve my goals without experiencing a “learners block” (P.S: I don’t know if that’s an actual thing).

In this post, I’ll share what I learned today, from JavaScript basics like numbers, variables, and strings, to functions and conditionals. I want this series to be a clear roadmap for anyone looking to start from scratch, just like me.

docs.title: Introduction to JavaScript
docs.text:
I’m learning JavaScript through Alchemy University’s Learn JavaScript course, which is meant to help me build a strong foundation before diving into blockchain and Ethereum development.

JavaScript is a programming language that lets you talk to your computer and tell it exactly what to do. Let’s dive in!

docs.title: Numbers and Variables
docs.text:
A variable is a name we give to a value so we can store it and use it later. Think of it like giving a label to a piece of information in your program.

1. Single Variable

let age = 21;       // "age" stores the value 21
console.log(age);   // prints 21

Here’s what happens:

  • let → tells JavaScript we want a variable whose value we might change later.
  • age → the name of the variable.
  • 21 → the value stored in the variable.
  • console.log(age) → shows the value of the variable on the screen.

2. Multiple Variables

let x = 5;
let y = 10;
let z = 15;

console.log(x, y, z); // prints 5 10 15

You can create multiple variables at once. Each variable has its own name and stores its own value.

3. Using Variables Together 

let sum = x + y + z; 
console.log(sum); // prints 30

You can do math with the numbers stored in your variables. Here, JavaScript adds the numbers from each variable and stores the result in a new variable called sum.

docs.title: Booleans
docs.text:
let isSunny = true;
let isRaining = false;
console.log(isSunny);   // prints true
console.log(isRaining); // prints false

A Boolean is a value that can only be true or false. It’s useful when you want to represent something that has only two options.

Tip: Think of Booleans as yes/no answers for your program.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
A string is a type of data that stores text. Anything inside quotes (single or double) is a string.

  • Simple Strings
    let name = "Mariam";
    let greeting = 'Hello';
    console.log(name);     // prints Mariam
    console.log(greeting); // prints Hello
  • Combining Strings
    let message = greeting + ", " + name + "!";
    console.log(message); // prints Hello, Mariam!

Tip: Strings are like words or sentences in your program. You can combine them, change them, and display them on the screen.

docs.title: Mutable Variables (let)
docs.text:
A mutable variable is a variable whose value you can change later. We use let to create these variables in JavaScript.

Changing Text
let color = "blue";     // color starts as blue
console.log(color);     // prints blue

color = "green";        // now color is green
console.log(color);     // prints green

Tip: Think of let like a name tag you can rewrite whenever you need.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Comments are notes you write in your code to explain what it does. The computer ignores comments. They’re just for you or anyone reading your code.

  • Single-line comment starts with //
// This is my first comment
let age = 21;  
console.log(age);

  • Multi-line comment starts with /* and ends with */
/*
This is a multi-line comment
It can cover several lines
Use it to explain bigger parts of your code
*/
let color = "blue";
console.log(color); // prints blue

Tip: Use comments to remember what your code does or to explain it to someone else.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: A function is like a mini-program you can use to do something specific. Once you create it, you can use it anytime without rewriting the code.

docs.title: addTwo() – adds 2 to a number
docs.text:
function addTwo(number) {
      return number + 2;
    }

    console.log(addTwo(5));  // prints 7

How it works:

  • function addTwo(number) → creates a function called addTwo that takes one input called number.
  • return number + 2; → adds 2 to the input and gives the result back.
  • addTwo(5) → calls the function with 5 as input. The result is 7.

docs.title: multiply() – multiplies two numbers
docs.text:
function multiply(a, b) {
      return a * b;
    }

    console.log(multiply(3, 4)); // prints 12

Note: return a * b; → multiplies the two numbers and gives the result back.

docs.title: average() – calculates the average of two numbers
docs.text:
function average(a, b) {
  return (a + b) / 2;
}

console.log(average(4, 6));  // prints 5

docs.title: random() – gives a random number between 0 and 1
docs.text: console.log(Math.random()); // prints a number like 0.123456

docs.title: floor() – rounds a number down to the nearest whole number
docs.text:
console.log(Math.floor(4.9));  // prints 4
 console.log(Math.floor(7.1));  // prints 7

Tip: Functions help you reuse code, do math, and work with numbers and text more easily.

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text: A conditional is a way for your program to make decisions. It lets your code do one thing if something is true and another if it’s false.

docs.title: isEqual – checks if two values are the same
docs.text:
let a = 5;
   let b = 5;

   console.log(a === b); // prints true
  • === checks if the two values are equal and of the same type. If they are equal, it returns true.

docs.title: notEqual – checks if two values are different
docs.text:
let a = 5;
let b = 3;

console.log(a != b); // prints true
  • != checks if the two values are not equal. If they are different, it returns true.

docs.title: greaterThan – checks if a number is bigger than another
docs.text:
let a = 10;
let b = 5;

console.log(a > b); // prints true
  • > checks if the first number is greater than the second number. Returns true if it is, false if it isn’t.

docs.title: else – gives a result if the first condition isn’t true
docs.text:
let a = 3;
let b = 5;

if(a > b) {
  console.log("a is bigger");
} else {
  console.log("b is bigger"); // prints this
}

  • if checks the condition (a > b).

  • If it’s true, it runs the first block.

  • If it’s false, it runs the else block.

docs.title: else if – checks multiple conditions
docs.text:
let a = 5;

if(a > 10) {
  console.log("a is bigger than 10");
}

else if(a == 5) {
  console.log("a is 5"); // prints this
}

else {
  console.log("a is something else");
}
  • else if lets you check another condition if the first one is false.
  • You can add as many else if blocks as needed.

Tip: Conditionals are like decision points in your code; your program can choose what to do based on the information it has.

docs.title: Closing Thoughts on Day 2
docs.text:
Yayy, another day done, and I actually feel like I’m starting to get the hang of JavaScript. Playing around with numbers, text, and Booleans was way easier than I expected. Writing my first functions and seeing them work felt like a mini “aha!” moment.

I did stumble a few times, especially figuring out how let works when changing values, but that’s okay. It’s all part of learning. I’m excited to see how tomorrow’s practice will help me connect all these little pieces together.

For now, I’ll take a break, maybe review my notes, and just enjoy the fact that my code actually ran without errors today. Baby steps!
